summary: This informational memo gives proposed registration and administration procedures for Chinese domain names. Many common Chinese characters have variants, so most names have at least two forms, and equivalence between Simplified and Traditional Chinese is key. It builds on RFC 3743 and explains the IANA tables.

plainLanguage.summary: A Chinese name can be written in more than one way, because many characters have a Simplified and a Traditional form. RFC 4713 describes how a registry should handle that: when someone registers a name in one form, the registry works out the matching name in the other form and registers both.

subtitle: Registering Chinese domain names that exist in both Simplified and Traditional character forms.

tldr.problem: Many Chinese characters were changed in their forms during the last century, so a name written in Simplified Chinese and the same name in Traditional Chinese are two different strings, and a person registering one expects to own the other.
tldr.mechanism: Two IANA language tables map each character to its variants, and the registration procedure derives a Simplified form and a Traditional form from the submitted label, adding up to three records to the zone file.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document describing a procedure that CNNIC and TWNIC adopted for the CN and TW domains. The IESG note says it was never a candidate for any level of Internet Standard.

today: RFC 4713 is an Informational document from October 2006 and has not been obsoleted or updated. The IESG note records that it was not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, that the decision to publish it was not based on IETF review, and that readers should exercise caution in evaluating its value. The procedure it describes has been adopted and deployed by CNNIC for the CN domain and TWNIC for the TW domain.

sections.title: Why the Same Name Has Two Forms
sections.content:
With the standardisation of Internationalized Domain Names for Applications, domain names containing non-ASCII characters are included in the DNS, and users can reach the Internet in their own languages. Many languages have special requirements that the IDNA documents do not address. One way to deal with some of the remaining issues involves grouping characters that could be confused together as variants, an approach discussed in RFC 4290 and, for documents written in Chinese, Japanese or Korean, in the Joint Engineering Team guidelines of RFC 3743.

Changes were made in the forms of a large number of Chinese characters during the last century to simplify writing and reading. These Simplified characters have been adopted in some Chinese-speaking communities, while others continue to use the Traditional forms. On the global Internet, if IDNA were used alone, there would be considerable potential for confusion if the two forms were not considered together. Effective use of Chinese domain names therefore requires variant equivalence, as described in RFC 3743, to handle the character differences between the Simplified and Traditional forms.

Chinese variant equivalence is very complicated in principle. When it comes to the use of Chinese domain names, the basic requirement is to match the user perception of Chinese characters between the Simplified and Traditional forms. When users register Simplified or Traditional domain names, they will wish to obtain the other forms as well, and expect others to be able to access the site or other resources in both forms.

This document specifies a solution for Chinese domain name registration and administration that has been adopted and deployed by CNNIC, the top-level domain registry for CN, and TWNIC, the top-level domain registry for TW, to manage Simplified and Traditional Chinese domain name equivalence. In the terminology of RFC 3743, the solution is based on Internationalized Domain Labels.
sections.plainLanguage: Chinese characters were simplified during the last century, and both forms are still in daily use. Without a rule for this, the same website could be registered twice under two spellings, and a link sent by one user would fail for another.

sections.title: The Tables and the Names
sections.content:
The document adopts the terminology defined in RFC 3743, and cannot be understood without first understanding the concepts and terminology of that document, including the terminology introduced in its examples.

The document suggests permitting only a subset of Chinese characters in Chinese domain names and hence in the DNS. When it discusses Chinese characters it refers only to the subset in the first column of the current IANA registration tables for Chinese. Characters excluded from these tables are still valid Chinese characters, but the document strongly suggests that registries do not permit the registration of characters that are not listed in the tables. The tables themselves will be updated in the future if necessary.

A Chinese domain name label is an internationalized domain name label that includes at least one Chinese character. Such a label may also contain characters from the traditional letter-digit-hyphen set.

Two language tables have been defined, both based on the rules of RFC 3743. The Simplified Chinese Variant Table can be used for the registration of Simplified Chinese domain names, and its key feature is that the preferred variant is the Simplified character, the one used by users in Chinese mainland or defined in Chinese-related standards. The Traditional Chinese Variant Table is used for the registration of Traditional Chinese domain names, and its preferred variant is the Traditional character, the one used by users in Taiwan or defined in related standards. The original Chinese domain name label is the label that users submit for registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Two tables do the work: one says which character is preferred in Simplified Chinese, the other says the same for Traditional Chinese. Everything else is a label that contains at least one Chinese character, submitted by a user.

sections.title: Applying the RFC 3743 Model
sections.content:
The document adopts the same procedure for Chinese domain name label registration as the one defined for more general internationalized domain name labels in Section 3.2.3 of RFC 3743. The terminology and notation derive from that document. The character variant associated with an input character and a language table is abbreviated CV, and the selected preferred variant is abbreviated PV. The language tables used are those for Chinese as spoken and written in Chinese mainland, ZH-CN, and on Taiwan, ZH-TW.

The first column of the Simplified Chinese Variant Table is the same as the first column of the corresponding Traditional Chinese Variant Table, and so are the third columns of both tables. The character variant is therefore the same for both language tables after the third step of the RFC 3743 model, while the preferred variant is in Simplified form in one table and Traditional form in the other. As a result there will not be more than three records to be added to the zone file after applying the procedure: one for the original label, one for the Simplified Chinese form and one for the Traditional Chinese form. The procedure does not generate labels that contain a mixture of Simplified and Traditional Chinese as variants.

The set of languages associated with the input is both ZH-CN and ZH-TW by default. The preferred variant is Traditional in the Traditional table and Simplified in the Simplified table, and there may be more than one preferred variant for a given valid character.

The procedure uses the optional registry-defined rules provided in RFC 3743 for optional processing, with the understanding that the rules may vary for different registries supporting Chinese domain names.
sections.plainLanguage: Applying the shared registration model to the two tables produces at most three names for one submission: what the user typed, the same name in Simplified characters, and the same name in Traditional characters. The two forms are never mixed together in one name.

sections.title: Registry Rules for Plausible Combinations
sections.content:
While IDNA, and hence RFC 3743, processes characters one at a time, the actual relationship between a valid code point and the preferred variant is contextual: whether one character can be substituted for another depends on the characters with which it is associated in a label, or more generally in a phrase. Some preferred variants make no sense in combination with other characters, and those combinations should not be added into the zone file, which RFC 3743 describes as zone variants.

If desired, it should be possible to define and implement rules to reduce the preferred variant labels to only plausible ones. This could be done, for example, with some artificial intelligence tools, or with feedback from the registrant, or with selection based on the frequency of occurrence in other texts. To illustrate one possibility, the original Chinese domain name label could be required to be Traditional-only or Simplified-only, and if there is more than one preferred variant, the original label will be used as the preferred variant, instead of the preferred variant produced by the algorithm.

The tables in the IANA registrations follow the table format and terminologies defined in RFC 3743, so a complete understanding of RFC 3743 is needed for the proper use of those tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Converting characters one at a time can produce a name that makes no sense, because some characters only work in certain combinations. The registry can therefore apply extra rules of its own to keep only the combinations that are plausible.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document is subject to the same security considerations as RFC 3743, which defines the table formats and operations. As with that base document, part of its intent is to reduce the security problems that might be caused by confusion among characters with similar appearances or meanings. While it will not introduce any additional security issues, additional registration restrictions such as those outlined in Section 3 may further reduce potential problems.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole point of the variant tables is to stop two characters that look alike from causing confusion, and the extra restrictions on registration reduce that risk a little further.
